GUIDE FOR TREATMENT AND DISPOSAL OF EFFLUENTS OF COTTON AND SYNTHETIC TEXTILE INDUSTRY

0.

FOREWORD

0.1 This Indian Standard was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 28 February 1980, after the draft finalized by the Water Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. 0.2 The cotton textile industry is one of the largest on the industrial map of India. There are about 700 mills with a gross annual production of 8 000 million metres ( I 000 million kg ) ia the country. A large variety of cotton textiles, textiles made from synthetic fibres and cotton blended with synthetic fibres are produced by the mills. They are located mostly in large cities having a well developed sewerage system. But quite a large number of the mills are also located in cities and towns where there are no infrastructural facilities for collection, transport and disposal of their waste waters. 0.2.1 In recent years the textile industry has undergone modernization The manuincorporating the latest developments in textile technology. facture of textile fabrics from cotton, blended with man made fibres, constitutes a major development in the cotton textile mills. The quantum of such synthetic textiles and cotton-synthetic blended fabrics varies from mill to mill to the estent of 10 to 40 percent of their gross production. 0.3 The wet processes in textile mills require large volumes of water of high degree of purity and discharge equally large volumes of liquid wastes which are complex and highly variable both in regard to quantity The waste waters are generally discharged into the and characteristics. The ultimate disposal of sewers with or without treatment or on land. the wastes along with sewage may be either into streams or the sea or on agricultural land. 0.3.1 The waste waters from the smaller textile processing units are small in volume but carry a significant pollution load and they should, therefore, be discharged only after treatment. 3

IS : 9508 - 1980
0.4 The object \of this standard is to give guidelines on methods of treatment and clisposal of efIluents of cotton and. synthetic textile industry in order to reuse as much as possible the treated ehluent in the system, so as to reduce fresh make-up water requirement to minimum possible level and to prevent water pollution. The methods recommended have been selected taking into consideration the practicability of their adoption in this country. As better and more economical methods of treatment are worked out in future, revision of this guide will be taken up. 0.5 The extent of pollution of inland surface waters permitted by discharge of eftluents is laid down in IS : 22W1974*. l'he following Indian Standards lay down tolerance limits for industrial eflluents: IS : 2490 (Part discharged I )-1974 Tolerance into inland surface limits for industrial effluents waters: Part I General limits effluents discharged discharged discharged

IS : 3306-1974 Tolerance limits for industrial into public sewers (jut revision ) IS :. 3307-1977 Tolerance on land for irrigation IS : 7968-1976 into marine 0.5~1 The extent IS : 7967 - 1976t.

0.6 Methods of sampling and test for industrial effluents have been published in IS : 2488 (Part I ) - 1966$, IS : 2438 ( Part II ) - 1968:, IS : 2488 ( Part III ) - 1968$, IS : 2488 (Part IV ) - 1974: and IS : 2488 ( Part V ) - 1976:. 0.7 A bibliography of references is given in Appendix A.

1. SCOPE

1.1 This standard covers methods of treatment and disposal of waste waters derived from the processing of (i) cotton textiles; (ii) textiles made from synthetic fibres alone; and (iii) textiles made from cotton blended with synthetic fibres.

IS: 9508-1980 2. PROCESSES 2.1 General

INVOLVED

-- The manufacturing processes of cotton textiles consist of a series of unit operations which are complex and highly specialized. Their actual description is outside the scope of this guide. However, they may be broadly divided into two steps namely (1) fabrication of the cloth, and (2) processing and finishing. The details of the various processes are shown in Fig. 1.

2.2.1 In the case of fabrics made of synthetic fibres only and cottonsynthetic blends, the preparatory processes are limited to the following: a) Texturization, b) Spinning, c) Sizing, d) Weaving and and knitting.

2.3 Processing of Cloth -The grey cloth from the weaving section passes through a series of operations in the processing section, such as desizing, kiering, bleaching, dyeing and printing. All these processes are wet processes. The wet processing of fabrics made from synthetic fibres and cotton-synthetic blends consists of desizing, bleaching, dyeing, printing and finishing. 2.3.1 De&zing - The sizing material present removed by one of the followmg two methods: in the

` grey

cloth ' is

a) Desi&q z&h enzytnes - The cloth is steeped in malt or enzyme bath followed by an acid treatment. The enzymes act on starch and other materials to produce readily soluble and washable compounds. b) Desi;ing by grey sour - In this process the cloth dilute sulphuric acid and is followed by kiers. 6 is treated with

IS:9508- 1980
2.3.2 Kiering - The kiering process consists of boiling the cloth to remove grease, waxes, natural fats and other impurities by an alkaline solution containing 1 to 3 percent of caustic soda, soda ash, sodium silicate, sodium peroxide and other chemicals for several hours with the aid of steam. The process is carried out either on a batch basis as in some of the older mills or on continuous basis in special units like J boxes in the modern mills. The spent liquor is blown out followed by washing of the cloth with a large volume of water. 2.3.3 Bleaching - The fabric from the kiers subsequently under-goes bleaching with alkaline hypochlorite solution or chlorine or peroxide ( hydrogen peroxide is used for bleaching of delicate fabrics ), In peroxide bleaching, sodium peroxide, sulphuric acid, caustic soda and a soluble oil are used. Sometimes peroxide bleaching is carried out directly in the kier itself or as a second stage after the kier. The bleaching operation is followed by a wash with plain water and then by souring ( acid and sodium bisulphite ) to remove the last traces of alkali and chlorine. The fabric is then soaped and treated with ultramarine blue to improve its whiteness. The bleaching of synthetic fabrics is carried out only with mild bleaching agents like sodium chlorite. 2.3.4 Mercerization - The process consists of treating cloth with a cold concentrated solution of caustic soda (200 g/l ) and then washing with system. The strong profuse quantities of water by a counter-current caustic is reused. The fabric is then treated with a diluted acid solution to remove the last traces of alkali, followed by a second rinse with fresh Mercerization improves the strength elasticity, lustre and water. affinity for colours. 2.3.5 Dyeing -L The dyeing of cloth is carried out with a variety of dyes and dyeing processes which are briefly described below: are neutral substances and are applied to a) Direct dyes -These the fabric without any mordants. These are easy to apply, fairly fast to light and are stable for washing. b) Basic djes - These are neutral substances of colour base and are applied with an acid, like, tannic acid, as mordant followed by a solution of tartar emetic. These dyes are noted for their bright colours. c) Vat dyes - Vat dyes belong to she class of fast dyes which are insoluble in water but are applied with the aid OF powerfir reducing agents such as sodium hydrosulphite and alkali. The cloth is then exposed to oxidation by air or oxidizing agents followed by souring to neutralise the excess of alkali. The fabric is washed at the end of each operation. 7

IS : 9508- 1980
d) Sulkhur dyes -These applied along with followed by oxidation. a contain sulphur reducing agent compounds and arc like sodium sulphidt

e) Nufihthol dyes-The colour is developed on the fibre by a twc stage process consisting of (1) treatment with betanaphtho: and (2) diazotization. This is followed by hot soap and caustic soda. f) Developed dyes -. In this the dyeing is carried out in a reverse manner. The colour is first directly applied to the fabric and then treated with sodium nitrite and acid to convert it into the unstable azo dye. Next the stable form of the colour is developed in the fibre by the action of betanaphthol.

g) Dyeing of yarn -- In the mills the yarn is also dyed as such the requirements. Initial scouring is depending upon followed by bleaching and then each lot is dyed by circulating the dye liquor and subsequently finished and reused. The synthetic fibres do not have natural affinity for dyes and colours and hence the dyeing process is carried out n.t an medium elevated temperature and pressure in an acid containing acetic acid at a pH ran,re of 1 to 2 in special This is followed by scourmg with detergents and machines. soap. 2.3.6 PrintingPrinting of cotton textiles is carried out either by means of hand block printing or roller printing in machines. Different techniques are employed, depending upon the dye used. The colour is applied as a thick paste along with starch or gum and mordant. The printing of synthetic textiles and synthetic-cotton blends is followed by ageing, steaming and carbonizing. 3. WATER

for textile processing is large and varies from one mill to another and this depends on factors like: (a) source of water and its availability; (b) the quantity and quality of the fabrics produced; The water usage for and (c) the types of processing and its sequence. different purposes in a typical cotton textile mill and synthetic textile processing mill is given in Table 1. mills surveyed is shown in

The processing of yarn also requires equally large volume of water. Bulk of the water consumed is in the washing of the fabric at the end of each process. 8

4.3 Characteristics 4.3.1 Slashing Wastes - contain mostly starch and softeners and the material left over after completion of the slashing operation and washing. The waste volume is small, but has a high biochemical oxygen demand ( BOD ). 4.3.2 Desizing Wastes - consist of mostly of washings and contain colloidal and dissolved organic matter derived from the hydrolysis of starch by enzymes. The waste volume is small but has a high BOD which amounts to 35 to 50 percent of the total BOD. 4.3.3 h?er Wastes -`The spent kier liquor and the washings are dark brown in colour and are strongly alkaline. They contain caustic soda and suspended solids most of which are fragments of cotton. The wastes have high PH, total dissolved solids, alkalinity and BOD. The BOD of the kier liquor is about 30 to 35 percent of the total waste load. 4.3.4 Bleaching and Mercerizing Wastes -L These are small in volume but highly alkaline. The wastes contain organic matter and the chemicals used such as hypochlorite, chlorine, caustic soda and peroxide. The BOD load contributed by the wastes from bleach house is about 5 percent. 4.3.4.1 The wastes from mercerization is almost negligible both in regard to its volume and waste load which amounts to less than 1 percent of the BOD load. a large volume 4.3.5 Dyeing Wastes - The dyeing process contributes Its composition and characteristics are highly variable of waste water. and exert a high oxygen demand due to the organic matter of the dyes, reducing agents like sulphide, hydrosulphite, nitrite, acetic acid and soaps. The BOD contribution from the dye house is about six percent of the total mill waste. 4.3.6 Printing Il'astes -The waste water derived from the printing process consists of colours, starch, gum and oil used in making the pastes and soaps. The quantity of the waste streams is small but has a fairly high BOD and chemical oxygen demand ( COD). 4.3.7 Finishing Wastes - The finishing of the cotton a negligibly small volume of waste water containing tallow and salts, etc. fabrics contributes traces of starch,

5.0

EFFECTS

Waste waters from cotton textile industry are of highly polluting nature and affect the water quality in several ways. 5.1 pH Value - The high alkalinity of the wastes causes an increase in pH value. Any increase in pH value of the receiving stream greater than 9.0 will have an adverse effect on aquatic life. soluble dyes and colours present in the wastes will 5.2 Colour -The persist in the stream and interfere with penetration of sunlight essential for photosynthesis. 5.3 Turbidity - The colloidal organic matter in the wastes will increase turbidity of the water and along with the colours, dyes and oily scum The oily scum formed on the will produce an unsightly appearance. surface of water will interfere with the mechanism of oxygen transfer at the air/water interface. 5.4 Oxygen Depletion - The most serious effect of textile wastes on the receiving body of water will be depletion of dissolved oxygen. The organic matter in textile wastes like starch, dextrin and inorganic chemicals like sulphide and hydrosulphite and nitrite will exert an immediate oxygen demand, while dyes and colours will exert long term Such changes in the oxygen balance of receiving oxygen demand. streams will be deleterious to fish life and will also interfere with self purification. Toxic chemicals like sulphide, chlorine, chromium and aniline dyes will also affect the aquatic life. 13

6. EFFECTS OF TEXTILE CULTURAL LAND

WASTES

ON

SEWERS

AND

AGRI-

to high PH value, alkalinity and total 6.1 Effects on Sewers -Due dissolved solids, the textile wastes have a tendency fo; incrustation in the sewers. On the other hand, the sulphur dyes and sulphur compounds Hence it present in the wastes will gradually lead to crown corrosion. is desirable that process waste streams containing sulphur dyes and sulphides are excluded from the waste water discharged into the sewers. 6.1.1 Efects on Sewage Treatment Plants-The plant and machinery of municipal sewage treatment plants will be exposed to corrosive action The pumps and pipelines may caused by acids and hydrogen sulphide. be subjected to incrustation. In any case the cumulative effect of textile wastes on sewage treatment plants will be increased cost of maintenance and repairs. 6.2 Effects on Agricultural Land-Textile effects on land in many ways as follows: The suspended and colloidal matter soil by forming an impervious mat; wastes have adverse

7. METHODS 7.0 The

OF TREATMENT

AND

DISPOSAL
pollution abatement of

general approach to the problem of textile wastes is based on the following criteria: a) Reduction b) Recovery c) Reduction d) Treatment and e) Application in waste volume, and re-use of process chemicals,

in waste load by substitution of waste waters by primary of advance waste treatment 18

of process,chemicals, and secondary methods. treatment,

IS : 9508 - 1980 7.1 Reduction in Waste .VoIume by Segregation and Reuse of Water - Segregation of the relatively highly concentrated waste streams from the less contaminated streams and reuse of the latter often contribute towards greater economy in water usage and reduction in waste water volume, but the gross waste load in terms of kg/l of BOD and suspended solids will, however, remain the same. 7.1.1 The washing of the cotton fabric at the end of each process in a modern textile mill is the most water intensive operation and accounts for the maximum water usage which is of the magnitude of 90 to 135 litre per minute for continuous washing of the fabric which moves at a Besides every chemical process fairly fast rate of 10 to 20 kg per minute. requires a minimum of one rinse with adequate volume of water and likewise the bleaching process also heavily depends on the intermediate washing. Attempts to reduce water usage in a textile mill are directed towards reduction in the duration of each of the processing sequences. Use of counter current system of washing; systematic control of bleach baths, recirculation of washings and scouring wastes and reuse of dye baths often contribute towards greate: economy in water consumption. On an average reuse of water is possible to the extent of 20 to 40 percent in a cotton textile mill. 7.1.2 Good housekeeping and important steps towards reduction prevention of leaks in the waste volume. and spills are

7.2 Recovery of Process Chemicals - Recovery of the following chemicals used in the processing section contributes towards reduction in waste load: a) Recovery of synthetic sizing agents like carboxymethyl cellulose from, desizing waste liquor by chemical precipitation with metallic salts for example aluminium sulphate, and its conversion into sodium salt by treatment with caustic soda; from mercerizing and process waste by b) Caustic recovery concentration and evaporation and from other wastes like kier wastes by dialysis; and c) Recovery of dyes - In the vat dying process only about 65 to 75 percent of the dye is absorbed by the fibre and the rest is drained This category of dyes may be recovered and reused in the out. Similarly bright coloured lakes, lacquers, same dyeing process. etc, may be recovered from basic azo and reactive dye waste liquors by precipitation of their metallic derivatives. 7.3 Reduction of Waste Load

cellulose 7.3.1 Subslitution of Process Chemicals - Use of carboxymethyl ( CMC ) and polyvinyl alcohol ( PVA ) in place of starch used in sizing 19

IS : 9508 - 1980
of cloth, use of mineral acids; instead of acetic acid in dyeing process and use of non-biodegradable detergents instead of soap are suggested ways and means for the reduction in BOD load of combined textile wastes to the extent of 50 percent. 7.3.2 Process Modjfications - Modification of certain manufacturing processes in textile mills such as use of high speed machinery with alternative process chemicals have been redorted in literature to be beneficial in reducing pollutional load. 7.4 Treatment-The various methods employed In the treatment textile mill waste waters are briefly described in the following clauses. 7.4.1 Pretreatment of Wastes of

7.4.1.1 Equalization - Equalization of waste streams over a period of time is essential for regulation of waste and prevention of shock loads created by batch dumping of certain strong waste like the kier liquor. The effect of such releases is sudden increase in temperature, PH value, alkalinity and ROD. Such waste streams should be segregated and contained in holding tanks of adequate capacity and released gradually at a more uniform rate. 7.4.1.2 Primary treatment -This consists of (a) screening of wastes for removal of coarse floating and suspended material, and (b) grit removal for separation of heavier and readily settleable gritty material. 7.4.1.3 Neutralization of wastes -The optimum pH value range for biological treatment of waste lies between 6.0 and 9.0. Textile wastes are of free alkali and therefore strongly alkaline with high amounts neutralization of the waste for pH adjustment is essential prior to biological treatment. Dilute sulphuric acid, carbon dioxide or flue gas may be used. 7.4.1.4 Chemical treatment - Waste streams from bleaching and dyeing processes or composite mill wastes are treated with conventional ferric chloride and chlorinated coagulants like alum, ferrous sulphate, Chemical coagulation is very effective for removal of colour copperas. and colloidal organic matter like starch and gums. More recently, certain coagulant aids like polyelectrolytes are used in combination with chemical coagulants. Reports on studies carried out by various research organizations in the country and abroad on chemical treatment of textile wastes indicate that alum and ferrous sulphate can be successfully used for colour removal and BOD and COD reduction to a satisfactory level. The results of one of the research investigations are summarized in Table 10. Chemical treatment resultsin sludge production 20

e) Settling tank which may be either a fill and draw type unit for small textile mills or continuous flow type with mechanical desludging equipment for large waste volume, and f) Sludge drying beds.

Pretreatment of the wastes for colour removal will be mom advantageous from the point of view of light penetration. Pond depths in the range of 0.9 to 1.2 m with retention period in the range of 10 to 30 days are considered suitable. BOD loading could be of the sanle order as that of aerobic ponds treating sewage that is 340 kg/hectare/day BOl) removal effkiencies to the extent of 75 to 80 percent may be achieved and the BOD of the final effhlent will be in the range of 30 to 50 mg/ 1. 7.4.2.6 Final treatment - The treatment methods described above have the main objectives (a) removal of colour, (b) PH control, (c) removal of settleable and suspended solids, and (d) reduction in BOD and COD. 22

IS : 9508 - 1980 However, these treatment processes do not alter the dissolved mineral constituents and the cations. Textiles wastes have a high sodium content usually in the range of 89 to 98 percent and the effluents resulting from the aforesaid methods will not meet the requirements of IS : 3307-1977*. Therfore, from the point of view of agricultural utilization, treatment with gypsum is considered essential to reduce the percentage of sodium in the total cation content of the waste. 7.4.2.7 .il,!$lication of advanced waste treatment methods - Advance waste treatment methods for textile mill waste waters will be applicable for as a tertiary treatment stage, reclamation of water for reuse purposes, the following primary and secondary treatment stages. The methods which may be found suitable are: (a) activated carbon treatment, (b) reverse osmosis, and (c) electro-dialysis. 7.4.2.8 Treatment of wastes from small textile processing units - The methods of pretreatment of the wastes water consisting of chemical and biological treatment systems especially the low cost waste treatment systems described above are also suitable for the treatment of process However, it will be more economical to waste waters from textile units. provide a common treatment facility for a group of sucbunits. 8.
